text: A well-meaning developer opens a pull request changing customers dot sql to join directly against payments instead of going through the existing payment summary model — a real, common dbt mistake.

This is a join fanout. Payments can have more than one row per order, so joining orders to payments without aggregating first produces multiple rows per order instead of one, and the query still runs successfully.

The result isn't an error — it's a plausible-looking, silently wrong number. Lifetime value and number of orders both come out too high, by exactly the amount of duplication, for any customer with a multi-payment order.
This pull request triggers CI automatically. dbt build runs customers, and the existing unique test on customer id fails, reporting the real count: got 14 results, configured to fail if not zero.

Because this check is required to pass before merging, the merge button stays disabled. This broken model never reaches main, never reaches prod, and never reaches Power BI. Next: diagnosing and fixing it for real.
